subject: Cloud Computing
title: Serverless Databases
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Serverless Databases.

hook.text: Your database runs 24/7 but only gets queries for 2 hours a day. You're paying for 22 hours of nothing.

buildup.text: Serverless databases scale to zero when idle and spin up on demand. No traffic, no cost.

discovery.text: Aurora Serverless, Cosmos DB serverless, and Neon pause automatically when nobody's querying them.

twist.text: Cold starts hit databases too. The first query after inactivity can take seconds while the database wakes up.

climax.text: Serverless databases are perfect for dev environments and variable workloads. Production systems may need always-on.

punchline.text: Pay only when queries run. Idle databases cost nothing.

quiz.question: What is a trade-off of serverless databases?
options: Cold starts cause delays when the database needs to wake up after inactivity
They can only store text data, not numbers or dates
Serverless databases lose all data when they scale to zero

details.summary: Serverless databases automatically scale compute and storage with demand and charge only for actual usage. Aurora Serverless, Cosmos DB serverless, and Neon scale to zero when idle, making them ideal for variable or unpredictable workloads.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional databases require provisioning for peak capacity, wasting money during idle periods. Serverless databases match cost to actual demand, which is transformative for development and sporadic workloads.
takeaways: Compute scales automatically with query demand
Can scale to zero when idle, eliminating baseline costs
Ideal for variable workloads and development environments

faq.question: What is the cold start problem for serverless databases?
faq.answer: When a serverless database scales from zero, the first query experiences higher latency while compute resources are provisioned. This cold start can take seconds. Some services offer minimum capacity settings to avoid cold starts at a small cost premium.

faq.question: Are serverless databases cheaper than provisioned?
faq.answer: For sporadic or variable workloads, yes. For consistent high-throughput workloads, provisioned instances are often cheaper because serverless pricing per unit of compute is higher. The breakeven depends on how many hours per day the database is active.
